rows.why: Each customer-facing AI use is documented with its purpose, the public users it serves and their expectations, and the consumer laws and norms that apply to answers given directly to customers.
Requirements for the customer-facing AI (telling customers they talk to AI, never disclosing other customers' data, handing off to a person) are set before it is built or deployed.
The knowledge limits of the customer-facing AI and the questions it must not answer are documented and made clear to customers, so they know when not to act on an answer.
The topics, channels and customer groups the public AI may serve are deliberately narrowed, taking into account the likelihood of misuse and abuse by public users.
The customer-facing answers and actions that are high-impact and need human review or hand-off before they reach or affect the customer are identified and documented.
The likelihood and magnitude of harm from public attacks (prompt injection, abuse) and from wrong, harmful or leaked answers reaching customers are assessed and documented.

Before launch the customer-facing AI is tried in conditions like the real public channel (real customer phrasing, non-optimised use, AI disclosure and hand-off to a person), and the results are documented.
Live customer conversations are monitored for abuse patterns, brute-force or extraction prompting and unreliable answers, with alerts when behaviour departs from what was tested.
The customer-facing AI is tested to fail safely when asked beyond its limits or provoked, refusing or handing off rather than giving harmful answers to customers.
The public-facing AI is red-teamed and penetration-tested for prompt injection, jailbreaks, abuse and data leakage by outside users, and the results are documented.
Customer conversations and high-impact answers are logged with enough detail, and human reviews and overrides recorded, so what a customer was told can be audited and traced.
Answers given to public users are checked for disclosure of personal or confidential data, such as another customer's details leaking into a response.
Customers have a way to report wrong or harmful answers and appeal outcomes, and these reports are counted, categorised and used in evaluating the customer-facing AI.
Guardrails, business rules and throttling restrict what the customer-facing AI can say or do and separate untrusted public input from system instructions.
The customer-facing AI can be quickly switched off or bypassed to a human channel when it misbehaves, with set thresholds and named people who decide.
Incidents where customers received wrong, harmful or leaked answers are tracked, responded to, reviewed and communicated to the affected customers.
Customer complaints and negative feedback lead to measurable changes in the customer-facing AI's guardrails, scope and hand-off rules in its updates.
